introduction-its-always-the-network.core: 'It's the network' is the default accusation in incidents, often wrong and sometimes right. Without network telemetry, teams can't prove either way. Network performance monitoring measures latency, loss, jitter, throughput, retransmits and path changes between endpoints, from both synthetic probes and real traffic, so network problems are found or ruled out with data in minutes.

first_principles.problem: An app team and the network team argue for hours during an outage because neither has data about the path between services.
truths: The network is shared and invisible.

analogy.title: Road traffic sensors
analogy.story: Without sensors, every late delivery is blamed on traffic; with sensors you know whether the road or the driver was slow.
analogy.breaks: Roads are visible; network paths are hidden behind many providers.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows whether loss or latency exists on the path.

code.text:
nstat -az TcpRetransSegs TcpOutSegs     # retransmit ratio
mtr -rwc 100 db.internal                 # loss per hop
ss -ti dst db.internal | grep -o 'rtt:[^ ]*'

check.q: What host-level metric quickly hints at network loss?
check.a: TCP retransmission rate (retransmitted segments relative to sent segments).

key-npm-metrics-reference.core: Core NPM metrics: latency (RTT, and its p95/p99 not just the average), packet loss percentage (even 1% cripples TCP throughput), jitter (variation in latency, critical for voice and video), throughput versus capacity (utilisation), TCP retransmits and resets, DNS resolution time, TLS handshake time and path changes. Each has typical healthy ranges, and baselines matter more than absolute numbers.

first_principles.problem: A dashboard shows average latency only, hiding 2% loss that halves throughput.
truths: Different problems show in different metrics.
Small loss has big TCP impact.

analogy.title: Vital signs at a hospital
analogy.story: Pulse, blood pressure, oxygen and temperature each reveal different problems; one alone isn't enough.
analogy.breaks: Vitals have universal ranges; network baselines are per path.

example.title: Loss vs throughput
flow: MSS 1460 B, RTT 50 ms, loss 0.01% → ~23 Mbps per flow

check.q: Why does 1% packet loss hurt TCP throughput so much?
check.a: TCP treats loss as congestion and cuts its window, and throughput scales inversely with the square root of loss rate.

strategy-1-active-monitoring-synthetics.core: Active monitoring sends test traffic on a schedule: ICMP or TCP pings, HTTP checks, DNS queries, traceroutes and throughput tests from agents in many locations (offices, regions, cloud zones, ISPs). It gives continuous baselines even with no user traffic, detects path changes and outages before users report them, and can test third-party paths. It measures the probe's experience, not every real user's.

first_principles.problem: A regional ISP issue affects users in one country for an hour before anyone notices.
truths: Many vantage points reveal localised issues.
Probes may not match real traffic paths.

analogy.title: Mystery shoppers
analogy.story: Regularly visiting stores in each city reveals problems before customers complain.
analogy.breaks: Shoppers act like customers; probes may take different paths than real traffic.

code.text:
modules:
  tcp_db:
    prober: tcp
    timeout: 3s
  icmp_path:
    prober: icmp
# alert: probe_duration_seconds > 2× 7-day p95 for 10m

check.q: What's a key limitation of synthetic network monitoring?
check.a: Probes may take different paths or behave differently than real user traffic, so they can miss issues that only affect real flows.

strategy-2-passive-monitoring-packet-cap.core: Passive monitoring observes real traffic: flow records (NetFlow, sFlow, IPFIX, VPC Flow Logs) summarise who talked to whom and how much; host and eBPF metrics expose per-connection RTT and retransmits; and full packet capture (tcpdump, mirrored ports, TAPs) gives ground truth for deep analysis. It shows actual user and service behaviour but produces large volumes and raises privacy concerns.

first_principles.problem: Users report slowness that synthetic probes don't reproduce, because only certain real flows are affected.

analogy.title: Traffic cameras vs a sample survey
analogy.story: Cameras on real roads see actual traffic jams that test drives might miss.
analogy.breaks: Cameras don't record conversations; packet captures can.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Ground-truth evidence of retransmissions on a real flow.

code.text:
tcpdump -ni eth0 -s 128 -w /tmp/db.pcap 'host 10.0.4.12 and port 5432' -G 60 -W 5
# analyse retransmits
tshark -r /tmp/db.pcap -Y 'tcp.analysis.retransmission' | wc -l

check.q: Why capture only headers (-s 128) when debugging with tcpdump?
check.a: Headers reveal timing and TCP behaviour while limiting file size and avoiding capturing sensitive payloads.

the-invisible-enemy-micro-bursts.core: A micro-burst is traffic exceeding link or switch-buffer capacity for milliseconds, for example many servers responding at once to a fan-out request (TCP incast). Buffers overflow, packets drop and latency spikes, yet 1-minute or even 10-second utilisation averages show the link at 20%. Micro-bursts cause mysterious tail latency and retransmits in data centres.

first_principles.problem: p99 latency spikes randomly while every network graph shows links at under 30% utilisation.
derivation: Suspect bursts when **drops exist at low average**.

analogy.title: A doorway at a concert's end
analogy.story: The venue is half-empty on average, but everyone leaving at once jams the exit for a minute.
analogy.breaks: Crowds are visible; micro-bursts last milliseconds.

check.q: Why can a link show 20% utilisation and still drop packets?
check.a: Utilisation is averaged over seconds or minutes, hiding millisecond bursts that exceed capacity and overflow buffers.

detecting-micro-bursts.core: To catch micro-bursts, measure at millisecond resolution and look at symptoms. Use switch buffer and queue telemetry (streaming telemetry via gNMI at sub-second rates, vendor buffer monitoring, max-queue-depth counters), interface output discards and pause frames, host-side eBPF or NIC counters for per-millisecond throughput, and correlation with TCP retransmits and p99. Mitigations include deeper-buffer switches, ECN/DCTCP, pacing and staggering fan-out.

first_principles.problem: Standard SNMP polling every 5 minutes can't show why drops happen.

analogy.title: High-speed camera at the concert exit
analogy.story: Normal photos every minute miss the crush; a high-speed camera shows exactly when the doorway jams.
analogy.breaks: Cameras capture everything; telemetry has export limits.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Bursts visible; fix by jittering fan-out.

code.text:
bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:net:net_dev_xmit /args->len > 0/ { @bytes[nsecs / 1000000] = sum(args->len); } interval:s:1 { print(@bytes); clear(@bytes); }'
# reveals per-millisecond spikes hidden in per-second averages

check.q: Name two mitigations for TCP incast micro-bursts.
check.a: ECN-based congestion control like DCTCP (or pacing) and staggering or jittering fan-out requests (also deeper-buffer switches).
